docs.title: Linear Model Classes
docs.text: Direct model access outside of Polars expressions.

docs.title: Common Interface
docs.text:
All linear model classes share this interface:

from polars_statistics import OLS, Ridge, ElasticNet, WLS, RLS, BLS, Quantile, Isotonic
from polars_statistics import TheilSen, RANSAC, BayesianRidge, ARD, LARS, PassiveAggressive, MomentAccumulator

# Fit
model = OLS(with_intercept=True, compute_inference=True)
model.fit(X, y)  # X: 2D numpy array, y: 1D numpy array

# Properties
model.coefficients      # np.ndarray
model.intercept         # float or None
model.r_squared         # float
model.adj_r_squared     # float
model.std_errors        # np.ndarray (if compute_inference=True)
model.p_values          # np.ndarray (if compute_inference=True)
model.aic               # float
model.bic               # float
model.model_info        # dict — see "model_info" below

# Predict
predictions = model.predict(X_new)

docs.title: model_info
docs.text:
Every class on this page (plus every GLM Model Class) exposes model_info -> dict — {"model_type": str, "family": str | None, "link": str} — read from the fitted model's own upstream HasModelInfo implementation, raising if the model is unfit. family/link default to "gaussian"/"identity" for classes without an explicit family (e.g. OLS); some classes have no family concept at all (family: None).

Class model_type family link OLS "ols" "gaussian" "identity" Ridge "ridge" "gaussian" "identity" ElasticNet "elastic_net" "gaussian" "identity" WLS "wls" "gaussian" "identity" RLS "rls" "gaussian" "identity" BLS (lower_bound/upper_bound not both 0/unbounded-below) "bls" "gaussian" "identity" BLS(lower_bound=0.0) (non-negative least squares) "nnls" "gaussian" "identity" PLS "pls" "gaussian" "identity" Quantile "quantile" None "identity" Isotonic "isotonic" None "identity" Huber "huber" None "identity" TheilSen "theil_sen" None "identity" RANSAC "ransac" None "identity" BayesianRidge "bayesian_ridge" "gaussian" "identity" ARD "ard" "gaussian" "identity" LARS "lars" "gaussian" "identity" PassiveAggressive "passive_aggressive" None "identity"

BLS reports "nnls" vs. "bls" per upstream's own bound-based dispatch (a pure non-negativity constraint on every coefficient is treated as the NNLS special case) — this is not a separate constructor kwarg, it is inferred from the lower_bound/upper_bound you pass. See GLM Model Classes for the GLM-family model_type/family/ link table (Logistic/Probit/Cloglog share family="binomial" but differ by link).

docs.title: OLS
docs.text:
Ordinary Least Squares.

from polars_statistics import OLS

model = OLS(
    with_intercept: bool = True,
    compute_inference: bool = True,
    alias_tolerance: float = 1e-7,
)
model.fit(X, y)

# Inference getters (populated when compute_inference=True)
model.intercept_std_error, model.intercept_t_statistic   # float | None
model.intercept_p_value, model.intercept_conf_interval    # float | None, tuple[float, float] | None
model.conf_interval_lower, model.conf_interval_upper      # np.ndarray | None — feature coefficients

# Per-observation diagnostics
diag = model.augment(X, y, residual_type=None)   # dict: fitted/residual/std_residual/
                                                   # stud_residual/leverage/cooks_d/dffits/resid_type

alias_tolerance (default 1e-7, R lm's own tolerance): see Rank-deficient designs below.

.augment(x, y, residual_type=None): R broom::augment-style per-observation diagnostics — see ps.augment for the full field semantics; residual_type defaults to "response" for OLS/WLS.

docs.title: variance_factor / leverage_new (OLS, WLS, Ridge)
docs.text:
model.variance_factor()       # np.ndarray | None — (p+1)x(p+1) with intercept, p x p without
model.leverage_new(x_new)     # np.ndarray — leverage h_ii for new rows

variance_factor() returns the matrix that, multiplied by the residual variance (inv(X'X) for OLS, inv(X'WX) for WLS, the ridge sandwich A @ X'X @ A' for Ridge), gives the coefficient covariance. Returns None when the model was fit from moments (fit_from_accumulator) — the raw design matrix isn't available to compute it.

leverage_new(x_new) computes the hat-matrix diagonal for new observations (x_new @ variance_factor() @ x_new.T, diagonal only). Raises ValueError (never a faer panic) when x_new's column count doesn't match the fitted model's feature count. Returns NaN for moments-fits (same reason as variance_factor()).

docs.title: fit_from_accumulator (OLS)
docs.text:
Fit OLS from precomputed sufficient statistics held in a MomentAccumulator. Useful for streaming or distributed workflows where raw data is unavailable at fit time.

model = OLS(with_intercept=True, compute_inference=True)
model.fit_from_accumulator(accumulator)  # accumulator: MomentAccumulator

docs.title: Rank-deficient designs (OLS, WLS)
docs.text:
Since 0.8.0 (anofox-regression 0.5.21 #64), OLS and WLS alias rank-deficient designs like R's lm: columns are kept in their given order, and a column that is a linear combination of the intercept and the earlier kept columns gets a NaN coefficient (coefficients[j] = NaN) and is excluded from rank/n_parameters. When two or more columns are collinear, the later column in argument order is aliased — this holds for every solve_method ("qr", "svd", "cholesky") and is independent of column scaling (a scaled copy, e.g. x2 = 2 * x1, aliases exactly like an exact duplicate).

Previously, solve_method="svd" silently returned a minimum-norm split of collinear columns with no NaN flag, and "qr" aliased the earlier column of a collinear pair — both now match "cholesky" and R's dqrdc2 convention.

model = OLS(solve_method="qr").fit(X, y)   # X columns 1 and 2 are collinear
model.coefficients  # e.g. [1.49, nan] — column 2 (the later one) is aliased

alias_tolerance (default 1e-7, matching anofox_regression::utils::LM_ALIAS_TOLERANCE and R lm's own tolerance) controls how close to exactly collinear a column must be before it is aliased: a tighter tolerance (smaller value) aliases more columns, a looser tolerance (larger value) keeps more. The default reproduces the behaviour documented above exactly.

docs.title: Ridge
docs.text:
Ridge regression (L2 regularization).

from polars_statistics import Ridge

model = Ridge(
    lambda_: float = 1.0,
    with_intercept: bool = True,
    compute_inference: bool = True,
)
model.fit(X, y)

# Inference (readable for the first time at lambda_ > 0)
model.std_errors           # np.ndarray | None — sandwich SE: sigma^2 * A @ X'X @ A'
model.intercept_std_error  # float | None
model.t_statistics         # np.ndarray | None — None when lambda_ > 0
model.p_values             # np.ndarray | None — None when lambda_ > 0
model.variance_factor()    # np.ndarray | None — the sandwich A @ X'X @ A' matrix
model.leverage_new(x_new)  # np.ndarray — see the shared note above

lambda_ > 0 inference rule: std_errors/intercept_std_error are always the ridge sandwich standard errors (matching R). t_statistics/p_values are None when lambda_ > 0 — a classical t-test on shrunken/biased coefficients is not statistically valid. At lambda_ = 0, Ridge delegates fully to OLS inference (t_statistics/p_values populated, matching OLS to machine precision).

docs.title: hc_inference (Ridge)
docs.text:
Compute HC-robust (heteroscedasticity-consistent) standard errors and p-values for an already-fitted Ridge model. Supports HC0–HC3 sandwich estimators.

from polars_statistics import Ridge

model = Ridge(lambda_=1.0)
model.fit(X, y)
hc = model.hc_inference(X, y, hc_type="hc3")  # Returns dict with se, t_stat, p_value

Supported hc_type values: "hc0", "hc1", "hc2", "hc3" (default "hc3").

docs.title: fit_from_accumulator (Ridge)
docs.text:
Fit Ridge from precomputed sufficient statistics.

model = Ridge(lambda_=1.0)
model.fit_from_accumulator(accumulator)  # accumulator: MomentAccumulator

docs.title: ElasticNet
docs.text:
Elastic Net regression (L1 + L2 regularization).

from polars_statistics import ElasticNet

model = ElasticNet(
    lambda_: float = 1.0,
    alpha: float = 0.5,  # L1 ratio (0 = Ridge, 1 = Lasso)
    with_intercept: bool = True,
    compute_inference: bool = True,
)
model.fit(X, y)

docs.title: WLS
docs.text:
Weighted Least Squares.

from polars_statistics import WLS

model = WLS(
    with_intercept: bool = True,
    compute_inference: bool = True,
    alias_tolerance: float = 1e-7,
)
model.fit(X, y, weights)  # weights: 1D numpy array

model.variance_factor()    # np.ndarray | None — inv(X'WX); see the OLS note above
model.leverage_new(x_new)  # np.ndarray — weighted hat-diagonal leverage; see the OLS note above

# Inference getters (populated when compute_inference=True)
model.std_errors, model.t_statistics, model.p_values      # np.ndarray | None — feature coefficients
model.conf_interval_lower, model.conf_interval_upper       # np.ndarray | None
model.intercept_std_error, model.intercept_t_statistic     # float | None
model.intercept_p_value, model.intercept_conf_interval      # float | None, tuple[float, float] | None

# Per-observation diagnostics
diag = model.augment(X, y, weights=None, residual_type=None)  # weights=None reuses the fit's own weights

alias_tolerance (default 1e-7): same rank-deficiency tolerance as OLS — see Rank-deficient designs below.

.augment(x, y, weights=None, residual_type=None): same R broom::augment semantics as OLS.augment — see ps.augment. weights=None (default) reuses the fit's own weights rather than requiring them again.

Known limitation: WLS.hc_inference raises NotImplementedError — HC-robust inference is not yet implemented for WLS. Use OLS.hc_inference or Ridge.hc_inference instead.

docs.title: RLS
docs.text:
Recursive Least Squares (online learning).

from polars_statistics import RLS

model = RLS(
    forgetting_factor: float = 0.99,
    with_intercept: bool = True,
    initial_p_diagonal: float = 1e6,
)
model.fit(X, y)

model.initial_p_diagonal_value  # float — the P0 = delta * I value used

initial_p_diagonal (default 1e6, matching the upstream crate's own default — omitting it is identical to passing 1e6): sets the diagonal value delta for the initial covariance prior P0 = delta * I. A smaller value (e.g. 1e-3) is a "tighter" prior that measurably shifts early coefficient estimates toward zero before enough observations have accumulated; a larger value is a "looser" (less informative) prior. An invalid delta (negative or NaN) raises ValueError at .fit() time (never a panic).

docs.title: BLS
docs.text:
Bounded Least Squares.

from polars_statistics import BLS

model = BLS(
    lower_bound: float | None = None,
    upper_bound: float | None = None,
    with_intercept: bool = True,
)
model.fit(X, y)

docs.title: Huber
docs.text:
Huber M-estimator (robust regression).

from polars_statistics import Huber

model = Huber(
    epsilon: float = 1.35,
    alpha: float = 0.0001,
    with_intercept: bool = True,
    max_iter: int = 100,
    tol: float = 1e-5,
    compute_inference: bool = False,
    confidence_level: float = 0.95,
)
model.fit(X, y)

# Properties
model.coefficients      # np.ndarray
model.intercept         # float or None
model.scale             # float — robust scale estimate
model.epsilon           # float
model.outliers          # np.ndarray[bool] — down-weighted observations
model.n_outliers        # int
model.r_squared         # float
model.mse               # float
model.rmse              # float
model.n_observations    # int

# Inference (only populated when compute_inference=True; all None otherwise)
model.std_errors               # np.ndarray | None
model.t_statistics              # np.ndarray | None
model.p_values                  # np.ndarray | None
model.conf_interval_lower       # np.ndarray | None
model.conf_interval_upper       # np.ndarray | None
model.intercept_std_error       # float | None
model.intercept_t_statistic     # float | None
model.intercept_p_value         # float | None
model.intercept_conf_interval   # tuple[float, float] | None

compute_inference=True validates against R MASS::rlm(method = "XtX")'s covariance (the nine getters above). Default False keeps every getter None (no inference computed, faster fit). confidence_level controls the width of conf_interval_lower/conf_interval_upper/intercept_conf_interval — a narrower confidence_level (e.g. 0.90) gives a strictly narrower interval around the same point estimate.

docs.title: PLS
docs.text:
Partial Least Squares regression.

from polars_statistics import PLS

model = PLS(
    n_components: int = 2,
    with_intercept: bool = True,
    tol: float = 1e-6,
    scale: bool = True,
)
model.fit(X, y)

# Methods
predictions = model.predict(X_new)
latent      = model.transform(X_new)   # Project into latent space

# Properties
model.coefficients              # np.ndarray
model.intercept                 # float or None
model.n_components              # int
model.explained_variance_ratio  # np.ndarray (one entry per component)
model.r_squared                 # float
model.n_observations            # int

docs.title: Quantile
docs.text:
Quantile regression.

from polars_statistics import Quantile

model = Quantile(
    tau: float = 0.5,  # Quantile to estimate
    with_intercept: bool = True,
)
model.fit(X, y)

# Additional properties
model.tau              # float
model.pseudo_r_squared # float
model.check_loss       # float

docs.title: Isotonic
docs.text:
Isotonic (monotonic) regression.

from polars_statistics import Isotonic

model = Isotonic(
    increasing: bool = True,
)
model.fit(x, y)  # x, y: 1D numpy arrays

# Properties
model.r_squared        # float
model.fitted_values    # np.ndarray

docs.title: MomentAccumulator
docs.text:
Online sufficient-statistic accumulator for OLS and Ridge. Accumulate batches of data and pass to fit_from_accumulator to fit a model without materialising the full dataset.

from polars_statistics import MomentAccumulator

acc = MomentAccumulator(n_features: int, with_intercept: bool = True)
acc.update(X_batch, y_batch)  # Call repeatedly with data batches
acc.update(X_batch2, y_batch2)

# Fit OLS or Ridge from accumulated statistics
from polars_statistics import OLS, Ridge
model = OLS().fit_from_accumulator(acc)

Properties: 

acc.n_samples    # int — total observations accumulated
acc.n_features   # int — number of features

Example: 

import numpy as np
from polars_statistics import MomentAccumulator, OLS

acc = MomentAccumulator(n_features=2)
for chunk in data_chunks:
    acc.update(chunk[:, :2], chunk[:, 2])

model = OLS().fit_from_accumulator(acc)
print(model.coefficients, model.r_squared)

docs.title: TheilSen
docs.text:
Theil-Sen median-of-slopes estimator — highly robust to outliers (up to ~29% contamination).

from polars_statistics import TheilSen

model = TheilSen(
    with_intercept: bool = True,
    max_iter: int = 300,
    tol: float = 1e-3,
    univariate_pairwise: bool = True,
)
model.fit(X, y)

# Properties
model.coefficients      # np.ndarray
model.intercept         # float or None
model.r_squared         # float
model.n_observations    # int

univariate_pairwise (default True): for a single-feature X, use the classical Theil-Sen estimator — the median of all pairwise slopes (Sen, 1968). Set univariate_pairwise=False to use sklearn's spatial-median-over-subsamples estimator instead (the original behaviour for single-feature data; this is always the estimator used for multi-feature X regardless of this flag).

Rank-deficient design (anofox-regression 0.5.15 #50): a column that is exactly linearly dependent on another is aliased to NaN in coefficients (not a huge near-1e14 value) — the same aliasing convention used elsewhere in this library for genuinely rank-deficient designs.

Example: 

import numpy as np
from polars_statistics import TheilSen

X = np.column_stack([np.linspace(0, 10, 50)])
y = 2.5 * X[:, 0] + 1.0 + np.random.normal(0, 0.5, 50)
y[0] = 100.0  # outlier

model = TheilSen()
model.fit(X, y)
print(model.coefficients)  # ~[2.5]

docs.title: RANSAC
docs.text:
Random Sample Consensus — fits a model to an inlier subset by iteratively sampling random minimal subsets and identifying consensus inliers.

from polars_statistics import RANSAC

model = RANSAC(
    min_samples: int | float | None = None,  # Fraction or count of min samples per trial
    residual_threshold: float | None = None, # Max residual to count as inlier
    max_trials: int = 100,
    stop_probability: float = 0.99,
    stop_n_inliers: int | None = None,
    random_state: int = 0,
    with_intercept: bool = True,
    compute_inference: bool = False,
    confidence_level: float = 0.95,
)
model.fit(X, y)

# Properties — describe the inlier-only fit (anofox-regression 0.5.14 #35)
model.coefficients      # np.ndarray (fitted on inlier set)
model.intercept         # float or None
model.inlier_mask       # np.ndarray[bool] — per-observation inlier flag
model.n_inliers         # int
model.r_squared         # float (on inlier set)
model.n_observations    # int — now reports n_inliers, not the full sample size

# Inference (only populated when compute_inference=True; same 9 getters as Huber)
model.std_errors               # np.ndarray | None
model.t_statistics              # np.ndarray | None
model.p_values                  # np.ndarray | None
model.conf_interval_lower       # np.ndarray | None
model.conf_interval_upper       # np.ndarray | None
model.intercept_std_error       # float | None
model.intercept_t_statistic     # float | None
model.intercept_p_value         # float | None
model.intercept_conf_interval   # tuple[float, float] | None

# Inlier-OLS fit statistics (now meaningful — computed on the inlier subset)
model.adj_r_squared     # float
model.mse               # float
model.rmse              # float
model.f_statistic       # float
model.f_pvalue          # float
model.aic               # float
model.bic               # float
model.log_likelihood    # float

model.inlier_fit()      # OLS — a real fitted OLS instance on just the inliers

0.8.0 semantics (anofox-regression 0.5.14 #35): r_squared, n_observations, and every fit-stat getter above describe the inlier-only OLS fit (|residual| <= residual_threshold), not the full sample — n_observations equals n_inliers, not the original row count. residuals still covers every row (not just inliers). A constant-response design (sklearn's MAD=0 semantics) fits cleanly.

inlier_fit() returns a real, independently usable OLS instance (via PyOLS::from_fitted) fit on exactly the inlier rows — its coefficients, intercept, and std_errors match RANSAC's own to 1e-12. Use it when you want the full OLS API (e.g. .summary(), .leverage_new()) on the inlier subset.

Example: 

from polars_statistics import RANSAC

model = RANSAC(residual_threshold=2.0, random_state=42, compute_inference=True)
model.fit(X, y)
print(f"Inliers: {model.n_inliers}/{model.n_observations}")
print(model.std_errors, model.p_values)

inlier_ols = model.inlier_fit()
print(inlier_ols.summary())

docs.title: BayesianRidge
docs.text:
Bayesian Ridge regression with automatic regularization via evidence maximisation. Provides posterior mean coefficients and per-prediction uncertainty.

from polars_statistics import BayesianRidge

model = BayesianRidge(
    max_iter: int = 300,
    tol: float = 1e-3,
    alpha_1: float = 1e-6,   # Prior on noise precision (Gamma shape)
    alpha_2: float = 1e-6,   # Prior on noise precision (Gamma rate)
    lambda_1: float = 1e-6,  # Prior on weight precision (Gamma shape)
    lambda_2: float = 1e-6,  # Prior on weight precision (Gamma rate)
    with_intercept: bool = True,
    compute_score: bool = False,
)
model.fit(X, y)

# Properties
model.coefficients        # np.ndarray (posterior mean)
model.intercept           # float or None
model.alpha               # float — estimated noise precision
model.lambda_             # float — estimated weight precision
model.sigma               # np.ndarray — posterior covariance of weights
model.scores              # list[float] — evidence lower bound history (if compute_score=True)
model.r_squared           # float
model.n_observations      # int

docs.title: ARD
docs.text:
Automatic Relevance Determination (ARD) regression — sparse Bayesian model with per-feature precision hyperparameters. Automatically prunes irrelevant features by driving their precision to infinity.

from polars_statistics import ARD

model = ARD(
    max_iter: int = 300,
    tol: float = 1e-3,
    alpha_1: float = 1e-6,
    alpha_2: float = 1e-6,
    lambda_1: float = 1e-6,
    lambda_2: float = 1e-6,
    threshold_lambda: float = 1e4,   # Features pruned when precision > threshold
    with_intercept: bool = True,
)
model.fit(X, y)

# Properties
model.coefficients         # np.ndarray (posterior mean; pruned features are 0)
model.intercept            # float or None
model.lambda_              # np.ndarray — per-feature precision
model.active_features      # np.ndarray[int] — indices of retained features
model.r_squared            # float
model.n_observations       # int

docs.title: LARS
docs.text:
Least Angle Regression — efficiently computes the full piecewise-linear regularization path from null model to OLS.

from polars_statistics import LARS

model = LARS(
    n_nonzero_coefs: int | None = None,  # Stop when this many features enter; None = full path
    with_intercept: bool = True,
)
model.fit(X, y)

# Properties
model.coefficients         # np.ndarray (at stopping point)
model.intercept            # float or None
model.coef_path            # list[np.ndarray] — coefficients at each knot
model.alphas               # list[float] — regularization values at each knot
model.r_squared            # float
model.adj_r_squared        # float (0.8.0) — R convention, df = active coefficients + intercept
model.mse                  # float (0.8.0)
model.rmse                 # float (0.8.0)
model.model_info           # dict (0.8.0) — {"model_type": "lars", "family": "gaussian", "link": "identity"}
model.n_observations       # int

adj_r_squared/mse/rmse (0.8.0, anofox-regression 0.5.21 #65): use R's summary(lm()) convention, df = active coefficients + intercept. For the full LAR path this matches summary(lm()) exactly; for n_nonzero_coefs stopping early (the active-set df formula) or a fit without an intercept, rmse/adj_r_squared match OLS(add_intercept=False) fit on the same active features.

Example: 

from polars_statistics import LARS

model = LARS(n_nonzero_coefs=5)
model.fit(X, y)
print(f"Active features: {(model.coefficients != 0).sum()}")

Collinear columns (anofox-regression 0.5.19 #62): when two feature columns are exactly collinear (e.g. x2 = 2 * x1), LARS aliases the later column — its coefficient is NaN and the fit equals the reduced model without it — instead of a platform-dependent result that could previously raise on one architecture and fit on another.

docs.title: PassiveAggressive
docs.text:
Online Passive-Aggressive regression — updates only when the current prediction error exceeds epsilon (PA) or combines hinge loss with L2 regularization (PA-I / PA-II).

from polars_statistics import PassiveAggressive

model = PassiveAggressive(
    C: float = 1.0,                  # Regularization parameter (smaller = more regularization)
    epsilon: float = 0.1,            # Insensitive zone width
    variant: str = "pa",             # "pa", "pa1", "pa2"
    max_iter: int = 1000,
    tol: float = 1e-3,
    shuffle: bool = True,
    seed: int | None = None,
    with_intercept: bool = True,
)
model.fit(X, y)

# Properties
model.coefficients         # np.ndarray
model.intercept            # float or None
model.n_iter               # int — actual iterations until convergence
model.r_squared            # float
model.n_observations       # int

Example: 

from polars_statistics import PassiveAggressive

# Online-style update for large datasets
model = PassiveAggressive(C=0.1, epsilon=0.05, variant="pa2")
model.fit(X_train, y_train)

docs.title: Survival Model Classes
docs.text: Direct AFT survival regression model access outside of Polars expressions.

docs.title: AFT
docs.text:
Accelerated failure time (AFT) survival regression with right censoring, for any of the Weibull, log-normal, log-logistic or exponential error distributions. Models log T = x'beta + sigma * W for a fixed error distribution W — the parametrisation of R's survival::survreg. An observation contributes its density when the event was observed and its survival probability when the row is still censored.

from polars_statistics import AFT

model = AFT(
    distribution="weibull",              # "weibull", "lognormal", "loglogistic", "exponential"
    priors=None,                          # same format as PenalizedGLM's priors
    vcov_type="laplace",                  # "laplace", "sandwich", "naive"
    add_intercept=True,
    max_iter=100,
    tol=1e-9,
    compute_inference=True,
    confidence_level=0.95,
)
model.fit(x, time, event)   # event: 0/1 (bool, int, or float), any other value raises ValueError

predictions = model.predict_linear(x)        # Linear predictor (location of log T)
quantiles = model.predict_quantile(x, p=0.9) # p-quantile of the survival time
medians = model.predict_median(x)            # predict_quantile(x, p=0.5)
survival = model.predict_survival(x, t=5.0)  # S(t | x) = P(T > t | x)
cdf = model.predict_cdf(x, t=5.0)            # F(t | x) = 1 - S(t | x)

distribution: "lognormal"/"log_normal"/"log-normal" and "loglogistic"/"log_logistic"/"log-logistic" aliases are also accepted. "exponential" (or "exp") fixes scale = 1 (not estimated) — every other distribution estimates it.

event: right-censoring indicator passed to fit, positionally after time — 1/True for an observed event, 0/False for a right-censored observation. Any other value (e.g. R's 1/2 coding) raises ValueError rather than being silently misread.

docs.title: Fit statistics
docs.text:
model.coefficients       # np.ndarray — feature coefficients on the log-time scale
model.intercept          # float | None
model.scale              # float — sigma (1.0, not estimated, for distribution="exponential")
model.log_likelihood     # float — on the time scale, as survreg reports it
model.null_log_likelihood  # float — intercept(+scale)-only model
model.aic                # float
model.bic                # float
model.converged          # bool
model.iterations         # int
model.n_observations     # int — rows used (non-finite/non-positive time, or null time/event, dropped)
model.n_events            # int — observed events among n_observations
model.n_censored          # int — right-censored rows among n_observations

docs.title: Inference
docs.text:
model.std_errors           # np.ndarray | None — feature coefficients
model.z_values              # np.ndarray | None — Wald z-statistics
model.p_values               # np.ndarray | None — two-sided p-values
model.conf_interval_lower    # np.ndarray | None
model.conf_interval_upper    # np.ndarray | None

model.intercept_std_error    # float | None — read directly from upstream's AftInference, never recomputed
model.intercept_z_value      # float | None
model.intercept_p_value      # float | None
model.intercept_conf_interval  # tuple[float, float] | None

model.log_scale_std_error    # float | None — None when the scale is fixed (distribution="exponential")

Every inference getter is None unless compute_inference=True, and the intercept/log_scale getters are additionally None without an intercept / without an estimated scale.

docs.title: Covariance
docs.text:
model.vcov          # np.ndarray | None — full parameter covariance at the mode
model.information   # np.ndarray | None — penalised observed information at the mode

Parameter order for vcov/information: the intercept first (when fitted), then the feature coefficients, then log(scale) (when the scale is estimated) — so for a fit with an intercept and p features the matrix is (1 + p + 1) square.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from polars_statistics import AFT

np.random.seed(1)
n = 80
x1 = np.random.normal(0, 1, n)
x2 = np.random.normal(0, 1, n)
scale = 0.7
eta = 1.0 + 0.5 * x1 - 0.3 * x2
log_t = eta + scale * np.random.gumbel(size=n)
time = np.exp(log_t)
censor_time = np.random.exponential(scale=np.median(time) * 1.5, size=n)
observed_time = np.minimum(time, censor_time)
event = (time <= censor_time).astype(float)
x = np.column_stack([x1, x2])

model = AFT(distribution="weibull").fit(x, observed_time, event)
print(model.coefficients, model.intercept, model.scale)
print(model.n_events, model.n_censored)
print(model.predict_quantile(x[:3], p=0.9))

Validated against R survival::survreg on the anofox-regression 0.5.22 R reference fixture: coefficients/scale (1e-6), log-likelihoods (1e-7), and intercept/coefficient/ log(scale) standard errors (1e-5), across all four distributions.

Priors and the sandwich covariance — parameter order is [intercept, x1, x2, log_scale]:

import numpy as np
from polars_statistics import AFT

np.random.seed(1)
n = 80
x1 = np.random.normal(0, 1, n)
x2 = np.random.normal(0, 1, n)
scale = 0.7
eta = 1.0 + 0.5 * x1 - 0.3 * x2
log_t = eta + scale * np.random.gumbel(size=n)
time = np.exp(log_t)
censor_time = np.random.exponential(scale=np.median(time) * 1.5, size=n)
observed_time = np.minimum(time, censor_time)
event = (time <= censor_time).astype(float)
x = np.column_stack([x1, x2])

model = AFT(
    distribution="weibull",
    priors=[None, ("normal", 0.0, 1.0), ("normal", 0.0, 1.0)],
    vcov_type="sandwich",
).fit(x, observed_time, event)
print(model.vcov.shape, model.information.shape)
print(model.intercept_std_error, model.intercept_z_value, model.intercept_p_value)
print(model.log_scale_std_error)

docs.title: Test Model Classes
docs.text: Statistical tests available as model classes with .fit(), .statistic, .p_value, and .summary() methods.

docs.title: Common Interface
docs.text:
All test classes share these properties and methods:

test.is_fitted()    # bool: Check if test has been performed
test.statistic      # float: Test statistic value
test.p_value        # float: P-value
test.summary()      # str: Formatted summary of results

docs.title: Non-finite input handling (anofox-statistics 0.4.4+)
docs.text: All test classes raise ValueError ("non-finite value") on NaN input — they never silently drop it like the matching expression builders do. +/-Inf input is not rejected: rank-based classes (MannWhitneyU, WilcoxonSignedRank, KruskalWallis, BrunnerMunzel) rank +/-Inf the same way R does. Constant input (zero variance) yields a NaN p_value rather than raising or dividing by zero. This differs from the Polars expression builders (ps.mann_whitney_u, etc.), which filter out non-finite values with is_finite() before computing and never raise.

docs.title: TTestInd
docs.text:
Independent samples t-test.

from polars_statistics import TTestInd

test = TTestInd(
    alternative: str = "two-sided",  # "two-sided", "less", "greater"
    equal_var: bool = False,         # False = Welch's, True = Student's
)
test.fit(x, y)

docs.text:

from polars_statistics import TTestPaired

test = TTestPaired(
    alternative: str = "two-sided",

test.fit(before, after)

Brown-Forsythe test for variance equality.

from polars_statistics import BrownForsythe

test = BrownForsythe()
test.fit(x, y)

docs.title: YuenTest
docs.text:

from polars_statistics import YuenTest

docs.title: MannWhitneyU
docs.text:
Mann-Whitney U test (Wilcoxon rank-sum).

from polars_statistics import MannWhitneyU

test = MannWhitneyU(
    alternative: str = "two-sided",   # "two-sided", "less", "greater"
    continuity_correction: bool = True,
    exact: bool = False,
    conf_level: float | None = None,  # Hodges-Lehmann CI level, e.g. 0.95
    mu: float | None = None,          # hypothesized location shift
)
test.fit(x, y)

test.estimate   # float | None — Hodges-Lehmann shift estimate
test.conf_int   # np.ndarray | None — [lower, upper], shape (2,)

Hodges-Lehmann estimate/conf_int (anofox-statistics 0.4.5): validated on 126 R wilcox.test(conf.int = TRUE) reference cases. The asymptotic interval is root-found with the continuity correction applied; one-sided alternative values give an interval with an infinite bound; exact=True is honoured only for n1 * n2 <= 10,000 (above that, the normal approximation is used silently); an infinite observation makes estimate/conf_int NaN. Computing the CI on 20,000 observations per group completes in O(n) memory (previously O(n^2), ~3.2 GB).

Since 0.8.0, ps.mann_whitney_u returns the same values as trailing estimate/ci_lower/ci_upper struct fields (additive; statistic/p_value unchanged) — see mann_whitney_u and Mann-Whitney / Wilcoxon Output.

docs.title: WilcoxonSignedRank
docs.text:
Wilcoxon signed-rank test for paired samples.

from polars_statistics import WilcoxonSignedRank

test = WilcoxonSignedRank(
    alternative: str = "two-sided",
    continuity_correction: bool = True,
    exact: bool = False,
    conf_level: float | None = None,
    mu: float | None = None,
)
test.fit(before, after)

test.estimate   # float | None — Hodges-Lehmann pseudomedian estimate
test.conf_int   # np.ndarray | None — [lower, upper], shape (2,)

Hodges-Lehmann estimate/conf_int (anofox-statistics 0.4.5): same R wilcox.test(conf.int = TRUE) parity as MannWhitneyU above. The interval is computed on x - y (not shifted by mu); exact=True is honoured only for <= 300 non-zero differences. O(n log n) time, O(n) memory — 100,000 observations per group is fine.

Since 0.8.0, ps.wilcoxon_signed_rank returns the same values as trailing estimate/ci_lower/ci_upper struct fields (additive; statistic/p_value unchanged) — see wilcoxon_signed_rank and Mann-Whitney / Wilcoxon Output.

docs.title: Regression Diagnostics
docs.text: Tools for detecting multicollinearity, quasi-separation, influence and outliers, plus residual batteries for OLS and GLM fits.

docs.title: augment
docs.text:
One combined, row-aligned expression returning R broom::augment-style per-observation diagnostics for any of nine supported models — an alternative to composing the individual OLS residual/leverage/Cook's-distance functions below, and the only way to get these diagnostics for a GLM fit in one call.

Signature
ps.augment(
    y: Union[pl.Expr, str],
    *x: Union[pl.Expr, str],
    model: str = "ols",
    weights: Union[pl.Expr, str, None] = None,
    residual_type: str | None = None,
    add_intercept: bool = True,
    theta: float | None = None,
    var_power: float = 1.5,
    link_power: float | None = None,
    max_iter: int = 100,
    tol: float = 1e-8,
) -> pl.Expr

Parameters: - model (default "ols") — one of "ols", "wls", "logistic", "probit", "cloglog", "poisson", "negative_binomial", "tweedie", "gamma". - weights — prior weights; required (and only valid) with model="wls". - residual_type — "response", "pearson", or "deviance". Defaults to "response" for ols/wls and "deviance" for every GLM (matching R's broom::augment). - add_intercept (default True). - theta — fixed negative-binomial dispersion (model="negative_binomial" only); None estimates it from the data. - var_power (default 1.5) — Tweedie variance power (model="tweedie" only): 0 Gaussian, 1 Poisson, 2 Gamma, 3 inverse Gaussian. - link_power (default None) — Tweedie link power (model="tweedie" only). None uses the canonical link (1 - var_power), matching ps.tweedie() and Tweedie(link_power=None) — the same model the user fits with the same arguments. Pass an explicit value (e.g. 0.0 for the log link) to override it. - max_iter/tol — IRLS iteration limit/tolerance (GLMs only).

Returns: Struct{fitted, residual, std_residual, stud_residual, leverage, cooks_d, dffits} — see Augment Output for the R-name mapping (std_residual = rstandard, stud_residual = rstudent, leverage = hatvalues, cooks_d = cooks.distance). One row per input row (returns_scalar=False, like the *_predict expressions).

NA handling: rows with a null/non-finite y, x, or (for wls) weights entry come back NaN in every field; the remaining rows equal a fit computed without that row — this is not an error condition, it is standard broom behaviour (a dropped observation legitimately changes every remaining row's leverage/Cook's distance/etc.).

R equivalent: broom::augment(model, type.predict = residual_type, type.residuals = residual_type).

Cross-check: for model="ols", augment's leverage/cooks_d/dffits/std_residual/ stud_residual agree elementwise with ps.leverage/ps.cooks_distance/ps.dffits/ ps.studentized_residuals/ps.externally_studentized_residuals below.

PyModel equivalent: every model listed above also has a .augment(x, y, residual_type=None) method on its PyModel class (WLS.augment additionally takes weights=None, defaulting to the fit's own weights) — see Model Classes and GLM Model Classes. It returns the same seven fields as a dict of numpy arrays, plus a trailing resid_type key (the resolved residual_type string), and always describes exactly what that PyModel instance was fit with.

Example: 

import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import polars_statistics as ps

np.random.seed(0)
n = 50
x1 = np.random.normal(0, 1, n)
y = 1.0 + 2.0 * x1 + np.random.normal(0, 0.5, n)
df = pl.DataFrame({"y": y, "x1": x1})

result = df.select(ps.augment("y", "x1", model="ols").alias("aug")).unnest("aug")
print(result.head(3))

# Per-group diagnostics
grouped = pl.DataFrame({"group": ["A"] * n, "y": y, "x1": x1}).group_by("group").agg(
    ps.augment("y", "x1", model="ols").alias("aug")
)

docs.title: condition_number
docs.text:
Compute condition number diagnostics to detect multicollinearity in design matrices.

ps.condition_number(
    *x: Union[pl.Expr, str],
    with_intercept: bool = True,
) -> pl.Expr

Returns: See Condition Number Output

Example: 

df.select(ps.condition_number("x1", "x2", "x3").alias("diagnostics"))

Interpretation:

Condition Number Severity Recommendation < 30 Well-conditioned Numerically stable 30 - 100 Moderate Monitor for instability 100 - 1000 High Consider regularization or removing predictors > 1000 Severe Strong multicollinearity present

docs.title: check_binary_separation
docs.text:
Detect quasi-separation in binary response data (logistic/probit regression).

ps.check_binary_separation(
    y: Union[pl.Expr, str],      # Binary (0/1)
    *x: Union[pl.Expr, str],
) -> pl.Expr

Returns: See Separation Check Output

Example: 

df.select(ps.check_binary_separation("success", "predictor1", "predictor2"))

Separation Types: - Complete: Predictor perfectly divides the classes (MLE does not exist) - Quasi: Nearly perfect separation with 1-2 observations crossing - MonotonicResponse: Each predictor level has all observations in same class

When Separation is Detected: - Consider using penalized regression (lambda_ > 0) - Remove or combine problematic predictors - Use Firth's bias-reduced logistic regression (if available)

docs.title: check_count_sparsity
docs.text:
Detect sparsity-induced separation in count data (Poisson/NegBin regression).

ps.check_count_sparsity(

    *x: Union[pl.Expr, str],
) -> pl.Expr

Returns: See Separation Check Output

Example: 

df.select(ps.check_count_sparsity("count", "x1", "x2"))

When Sparsity is Detected: - Use regularization (lambda_ > 0) - Consider zero-inflated models - Check for sparse predictor-response combinations

docs.title: vif
docs.text:
Variance Inflation Factor per predictor: VIF_j = 1 / (1 - R²_j).

ps.vif(*x: Union[pl.Expr, str]) -> pl.Expr

Returns: See VIF Output

Example: 

df.select(ps.vif("x1", "x2", "x3").alias("vif"))

VIF > 5 (moderate) / > 10 (severe) typically flags problematic collinearity. The intercept is not included.

ps.generalized_vif(

Example: 

# x1, x2 are scalars; cat_a/cat_b/cat_c are dummies for one categorical
df.select(

docs.title: Diagnostic Workflow
docs.text:
import polars as pl
import polars_statistics as ps

# 1. Check multicollinearity before fitting
cond = df.select(ps.condition_number("x1", "x2", "x3"))
vif = df.select(ps.vif("x1", "x2", "x3"))

# 2. For binary outcomes, check separation
sep = df.select(ps.check_binary_separation("y", "x1", "x2"))
if sep["separation"][0]["has_separation"]:
    model = df.select(ps.logistic("y", "x1", "x2", lambda_=1.0))
else:
    model = df.select(ps.logistic("y", "x1", "x2"))

# 3. After fitting OLS, scan for outliers and influential points
df.select(ps.residual_outliers("y", "x1", "x2").alias("outliers"))
df.select(ps.influential_cooks("y", "x1", "x2").alias("influence"))

# 4. Or get the full per-observation diagnostic battery in one call (OLS or any GLM)
df.select(ps.augment("y", "x1", "x2", model="ols").alias("aug")).unnest("aug")

Note: The list-shaped OLS diagnostics above (leverage, cooks_distance, dffits, studentized_residuals, externally_studentized_residuals) and augment's equivalent row-aligned fields agree elementwise for the same data — they are two different shapes (List[Float64] per call vs. one Struct row per observation) over the same underlying computation, not two different implementations.

docs.title: Dynamic Linear Model (LmDynamic)
docs.text: Time-varying coefficient regression using information criterion-weighted model averaging with optional LOWESS smoothing.

docs.title: lm_dynamic
docs.text:
ps.lm_dynamic(
    y: Union[pl.Expr, str],
    *x: Union[pl.Expr, str],
    ic: str = "aicc",              # "aic", "aicc", "bic"
    distribution: str = "normal",  # "normal", "laplace", "student_t", etc.
    lowess_span: float = 0.3,      # LOWESS smoothing span (0.05-1.0)
    max_models: int = 64,          # Max candidate models
    with_intercept: bool = True,
) -> pl.Expr

Returns: See LmDynamic Output

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Description ic Information criterion for model weighting: "aic", "aicc" (default), or "bic" distribution Error distribution for ALM fitting lowess_span LOWESS smoothing bandwidth (0.05-1.0). Lower = more local, Higher = smoother max_models Maximum number of candidate models to consider

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Model Generation: Creates candidate models with different predictor subsets
  2. Per-Observation IC: Computes information criterion values at each observation
  3. Model Weighting: Weights models based on IC values (Akaike weights)
  4. Coefficient Averaging: Combines coefficients using weights at each time point
  5. LOWESS Smoothing: Optionally smooths the time-varying weights

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
# Fit dynamic model per group
result = df.group_by("group").agg(
    ps.lm_dynamic("y", "x1", "x2", lowess_span=0.3).alias("model")
).unnest("model")

# Access time-varying coefficients (via model class)
from polars_statistics import LmDynamic
model = LmDynamic(lowess_span=0.3)
model.fit(X, y)
print(model.dynamic_coefficients)  # (n_obs x n_coef) array

docs.title: Formula Syntax
docs.text:
Formula-based regression using R-style syntax. Supports polynomial and interaction effects that are computed per-group with group_by/over.

Note: Unlike R, the intercept is controlled via the with_intercept parameter, not in the formula. R's y ~ x - 1 or y ~ 0 + x syntax for removing the intercept is not supported. Use with_intercept=False instead.

docs.title: Penalized IRLS
docs.text:
All GLM expressions (logistic, poisson, negative_binomial, tweedie, probit, cloglog) accept a lambda_ kwarg (default 0.0) that adds an L2 (ridge) penalty on the coefficients inside the IRLS update. Set lambda_ > 0 to stabilize estimation under collinearity or quasi-separation.

The sklearn-style logistic_regression exposes the same penalty via C = 1 / lambda_ and an explicit penalty choice.

estimate_dispersion (default False): scales the coefficient std_error by the Pearson chi2/df dispersion estimate, matching R summary.glm for negative-binomial fits (anofox-regression 0.5.15 #49). With the default False, dispersion is fixed at 1.0 (R's own default). Also available on negative_binomial_summary, negative_binomial_predict, and negative_binomial_formula. docs.title: tweedie
docs.text:
Tweedie GLM for flexible variance structures.

ps.tweedie(
    y: Union[pl.Expr, str],
    *x: Union[pl.Expr, str],
    var_power: float = 1.5,      # 0=Gaussian, 1=Poisson, 2=Gamma, 3=InvGaussian
    lambda_: float = 0.0,        # L2 (Ridge) regularization strength
    with_intercept: bool = True,
) -> pl.Expr

Returns: See GLM Output

Variance Power Interpretation: | var_power | Distribution | |-----------|--------------| | 0 | Gaussian (Normal) | | 1 | Poisson | | (1, 2) | Compound Poisson-Gamma | | 2 | Gamma | | 3 | Inverse Gaussian |

aic/bic are NaN for non-closed-form var_power. A closed-form Tweedie density (and therefore a well-defined likelihood) exists only for var_power in {0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0}. The default var_power=1.5 (compound Poisson-Gamma) has no closed-form density, so aic/bic are NaN by design — this is not a bug. See GLM Output and Tweedie for the full behaviour.

docs.title: Linear Regression Models
docs.text:
Standard linear regression models including OLS, Ridge, Elastic Net, and specialized variants.

Behaviour changes in 0.8.0

The upstream anofox-regression 0.5.14/0.5.15 releases bundled in polars-statistics 0.8.0 changed several linear-solver statistics to match R:

  • log_likelihood/aic/bic now equal R's logLik.lm/AIC/BIC (ML variance RSS / n, k = p + 1 parameters) for ols and the other linear solvers — previously a different (non-R-matching) formula.
  • No-intercept r_squared/adj_r_squared/f_statistic now use the uncentred total sum of squares, matching R summary.lm's own no-intercept convention, for both ols and wls.
  • A constant column without with_intercept is no longer aliased to NaN — it now behaves exactly like an explicit intercept term.

alias_tolerance (0.8.0)

ols/wls (and their _summary/_predict/formula variants) accept an alias_tolerance: float = 1e-7 kwarg — R lm's configurable rank-deficiency tolerance (anofox_regression::utils::LM_ALIAS_TOLERANCE). A later column that is a linear combination of the intercept and earlier kept columns within this tolerance is aliased (NaN coefficient, excluded from rank/n_parameters); a tighter tolerance (smaller value) aliases more columns, a looser tolerance (larger value) keeps more. The default reproduces the pre-0.8.0 behaviour exactly. See Rank-deficient designs for the full column-ordering/aliasing semantics this tolerance controls.

docs.title: Penalized GLM
docs.text:
One IRLS engine shared by Poisson, Binomial, Logistic, Negative Binomial, Gamma and Tweedie regression, with optional explicit per-coefficient priors (Gaussian/Laplace), a uniform ridge penalty (lambda_), offsets, and a selectable covariance at the mode. Without priors and with lambda_ = 0.0 this is a plain maximum-likelihood GLM matching R's glm / MASS::glm.nb; with Gaussian priors it returns the posterior mode (as arm::bayesglm with fixed prior scales). Validated against R glm / MASS::glm.nb on the anofox-regression 0.5.22 R reference fixture.

Works with group_by and .over().

docs.title: Families and Links
docs.text:
family Links (link=) Notes "poisson" "log" (default), "identity", "sqrt" estimate_dispersion is only valid here "binomial" "logit" (default), "probit", "cloglog" "logistic" "logit" only Adds a classification threshold and the accuracy output field "negative_binomial" "log" only theta fixed or ML-estimated (None) "gamma" "log" only "tweedie" "log" only power in [1, 2], default 1.5

An invalid link for the chosen family, or theta/power/threshold supplied for the wrong family, raises ValueError when the expression is built — before .collect().

docs.title: Dispersion
docs.text:
Poisson fixes dispersion at 1.0 by default, exactly like R's glm(family = poisson). Setting estimate_dispersion=True scales the coefficient covariance (and therefore the standard errors, z-statistics, p-values, and confidence intervals) by the Pearson chi2/df dispersion estimate — R's quasipoisson family. estimate_dispersion is Poisson-only; every other family fixes its own dispersion rule and rejects the option with ValueError.

Gamma and Tweedie always use the Pearson dispersion estimate (never fixed at 1.0). Gamma's log-likelihood and aic/bic are computed at deviance/n, matching R's logLik.glm. Tweedie's aic/bic are NaN unless power is one of 0.0, 1.0, 2.0, or 3.0 (no closed-form density otherwise) — the default power=1.5 therefore has NaN aic/bic by design.

import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import polars_statistics as ps

np.random.seed(0)
n = 80
x1 = np.random.normal(0, 1, n)
mu = np.exp(0.3 + 0.5 * x1)
y = np.random.poisson(mu).astype(float)
df = pl.DataFrame({"y": y, "x1": x1})

# Fixed dispersion = 1.0 (R's glm(family = poisson) default)
default_fit = df.select(ps.penalized_glm("y", "x1", family="poisson").alias("m"))
print(default_fit["m"][0]["dispersion"])  # 1.0

# Quasipoisson: scale the covariance by the Pearson chi2/df estimate
quasi_fit = df.select(
    ps.penalized_glm("y", "x1", family="poisson", estimate_dispersion=True).alias("m")
)
print(quasi_fit["m"][0]["dispersion"])  # Pearson chi2/df, e.g. ~1.13

docs.title: Priors
docs.text:
priors accepts a sequence positionally aligned with the feature columns (*x). Each entry is:

  • None or "flat" — flat (uninformative) prior, the default for every coefficient.
  • A (kind, loc, scale) tuple/list (or (kind,)/(kind, loc)), or a dict {"kind", "loc", "scale"} — kind is one of "flat", "normal", "laplace".

An optional leading entry applies to the intercept, so priors may have p entries (one per feature) or p + 1 entries (intercept first, then one per feature).

  • "normal" (Gaussian): an L2 penalty with standard deviation scale — a ridge-like prior. With lambda_ = L, a ("normal", 0.0, 1 / sqrt(L)) prior on every non-intercept coefficient gives numerically identical coefficients to the uniform ridge penalty.
  • "laplace": an L1 penalty with scale b — can proximal-soft-threshold a coefficient to exactly 0.0. A coefficient zeroed this way has NaN in std_errors/ci_lower/ci_upper (no curvature-based standard error exists for an inactive L1 coefficient).
import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import polars_statistics as ps

np.random.seed(0)
n = 80
x1 = np.random.normal(0, 1, n)
x2 = np.random.normal(0, 1, n)
mu = np.exp(0.3 + 0.5 * x1 - 0.2 * x2)
y = np.random.poisson(mu).astype(float)
df = pl.DataFrame({"y": y, "x1": x1, "x2": x2})

# Gaussian priors (ridge-like, posterior mode) on x1 and x2; flat on the intercept
result = df.select(
    ps.penalized_glm(
        "y", "x1", "x2",
        family="poisson",
        priors=[None, ("normal", 0.0, 1.0), ("normal", 0.0, 1.0)],
    ).alias("model")
)
print(result["model"][0]["coefficients"])

docs.title: Covariance types
docs.text:
vcov_type (on penalized_glm_summary; PenalizedGLM.vcov on the PyModel) selects the covariance at the mode:

vcov_type Formula Use case "laplace" (default) (X'WX + P)^-1 The Laplace approximation — the correct observed information for a MAP estimate "sandwich" sandwich estimator Targets the frequentist sampling variance of the penalized estimator "naive" (X'WX)^-1 Ignores the penalty entirely

All three coincide for an unpenalized fit (no priors, lambda_ = 0.0).

docs.title: Offsets
docs.text:
offset adds a known quantity to the linear predictor on the link scale — e.g. log(exposure) for a Poisson rate model — and defaults to a constant 0.0 column. Null deviance follows R's glm behaviour with an offset present or with add_intercept=False. A null offset value always yields a NaN prediction from penalized_glm_predict, regardless of null_policy.

import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import polars_statistics as ps

np.random.seed(0)
n = 80
x1 = np.random.normal(0, 1, n)
exposure = np.random.uniform(0.5, 2.0, n)
mu = exposure * np.exp(0.3 + 0.5 * x1)
y = np.random.poisson(mu).astype(float)
df = pl.DataFrame({"y": y, "x1": x1, "exposure": exposure})

result = df.select(
    ps.penalized_glm("y", "x1", family="poisson", offset=pl.col("exposure").log()).alias("m")
)
print(result["m"][0]["intercept"])

docs.text:
ps.penalized_glm(
    y: Union[pl.Expr, str],
    *x: Union[pl.Expr, str],
    family: Literal["poisson", "binomial", "logistic", "negative_binomial", "gamma", "tweedie"] = "poisson",
    link: str | None = None,
    theta: float | None = None,
    power: float | None = None,
    threshold: float = 0.5,
    lambda_: float = 0.0,

    offset: Union[pl.Expr, str, None] = None,
    add_intercept: bool = True,
    max_iter: int = 100,
    tol: float = 1e-8,
) -> pl.Expr
Parameter Description family Response family; see Families and Links link Link function; defaults to the family's canonical link theta Fixed Negative Binomial dispersion; None estimates it by ML (family="negative_binomial" only) power Tweedie variance power in [1, 2]; default 1.5 (family="tweedie" only) threshold Classification threshold in (0, 1) (family="logistic" only) lambda_ Uniform L2 ridge penalty on non-intercept coefficients, composed additively with priors estimate_dispersion Poisson-only quasipoisson dispersion scaling; see Dispersion priors Per-coefficient priors; see Priors offset Offset column/expression on the link scale; defaults to 0.0; see Offsets add_intercept Whether to include an intercept term max_iter Maximum IRLS iterations tol Convergence tolerance

docs.title: Empirical-Bayes Shrinkage
docs.text:
Empirical-Bayes (random-effects meta-analytic) shrinkage of per-group estimates toward a pooled mean, matching R's metafor::rma(method = "DL") / blup(). Pulls noisy, low-precision estimates toward the overall mean while leaving precise estimates nearly untouched — the classic James-Stein / DerSimonian-Laird shrinkage estimator.

Validation: Validated against R metafor::rma(method = "DL")/blup() on the metafor::dat.bcg reference dataset and additional synthetic fixtures.

Works with group_by and .over().

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
Given k groups' point estimates y_i and their standard errors se_i, the random-effects model is y_i = mu + u_i + e_i, where u_i ~ N(0, tau_squared) (between-group heterogeneity) and e_i ~ N(0, se_i^2) (within-group sampling error, known). eb_shrink estimates tau_squared (DerSimonian-Laird by default), then computes the pooled mean mu and, for each row, the empirical-Bayes shrunken estimate (the best linear unbiased predictor, BLUP):

weight_i    = 1 / (se_i^2 + tau_squared)
mu          = sum(weight_i * y_i) / sum(weight_i)          # inverse-variance pooled mean
shrunken_i  = weight_i * se_i^2 * mu + (1 - weight_i * se_i^2) * y_i
            = y_i - se_i^2 / (se_i^2 + tau_squared) * (y_i - mu)

A group with a large se_i (noisy) gets pulled strongly toward mu; a group with a small se_i (precise) stays close to its own y_i. When tau_squared == 0 every group is pulled all the way to mu (complete pooling); as tau_squared -> infinity, shrunken_i -> y_i (no pooling).

docs.title: eb_shrink
docs.text:
Signature
ps.eb_shrink(
    estimate: pl.Expr | str,
    std_error: pl.Expr | str,
    method: str = "dl",
    tau_squared: float | None = None,
) -> pl.Expr

Parameters: - estimate — per-row point estimate (e.g. a per-store/per-study effect size), or a column name. - std_error — per-row standard error of estimate, or a column name. Must be positive and finite; non-positive or non-finite values mark the row unusable. - method (default "dl") — "dl" estimates tau_squared via DerSimonian-Laird (matching metafor::rma(method = "DL")); "none" forces tau_squared = 0 (complete pooling — every shrunken value equals mu). - tau_squared (default None) — if given, overrides the estimator entirely and uses this fixed value instead of estimating it from the data. Must be finite and >= 0.

Returns: Struct{shrunken, shrunken_se, weight, mu, mu_se, tau_squared, i_squared, q, n_groups} — see EB Shrinkage Output for the full field table. One row per input row (returns_scalar=False, like the *_predict expressions) — every shrunken value belongs to an input row, unlike the one-row List[Struct] shape used by the post-hoc pairwise tests. mu/mu_se/tau_squared/i_squared/q/ n_groups are whole-sample scalars, repeated identically on every row.

R equivalent: rma(yi = estimate, sei = std_error, method = "DL") for mu/tau_squared/ q/i_squared, then blup(fit)$pred/blup(fit)$se for shrunken/shrunken_se.

Notes: - i_squared is the Higgins-Thompson I^2 (the proportion of total variation due to heterogeneity rather than sampling error), not an alternative heterogeneity measure. - q is Cochran's Q heterogeneity test statistic. - Rows with a null/non-finite estimate, or a non-positive/non-finite std_error, stay NaN-aligned (all nine fields NaN for that row) and are excluded from mu/tau_squared/ n_groups. Fewer than 2 usable rows (a single usable row, every row unusable, or an empty frame) give all-NaN rows with n_groups == 0 — never an exception. - ValueError is raised at build time (before .collect()) for an unknown method or an invalid tau_squared. - Use .over(family) (or group_by(family).agg(...)) to shrink several independent families of estimates within one DataFrame — each family gets its own mu/tau_squared.

Example — per-store estimates shrunk toward the chain mean: 

import polars as pl
import polars_statistics as ps

df = pl.DataFrame({
    "store": ["s1", "s2", "s3", "s4", "s5"],
    "estimate": [0.12, 0.35, -0.05, 0.40, 0.08],
    "std_error": [0.10, 0.30, 0.05, 0.35, 0.09],
})

result = df.with_columns(
    ps.eb_shrink("estimate", "std_error").alias("eb")
).unnest("eb")
print(result.select("store", "estimate", "shrunken", "shrunken_se", "mu", "tau_squared"))

Example — several independent families with .over(): 

import polars as pl
import polars_statistics as ps

df = pl.DataFrame({
    "family": ["a", "a", "a", "b", "b", "b"],
    "estimate": [0.12, 0.35, -0.05, 1.2, 0.9, 1.5],
    "std_error": [0.10, 0.30, 0.05, 0.40, 0.25, 0.50],
})

result = df.with_columns(
    ps.eb_shrink("estimate", "std_error").over("family").alias("eb")
).unnest("eb")
print(result.select("family", "estimate", "shrunken", "mu"))

Formula variants also available: ps.ols_formula_summary(formula, ...), etc.

penalized_glm_summary and aft_summary return a widened 7-field schema — the usual {term, estimate, std_error, statistic, p_value} plus trailing ci_lower/ci_upper (additive; the shared schema above and every other *_summary expression are unchanged). The intercept row is read directly from the upstream engine's own intercept inference, never recomputed locally. See Inference Summary Output, Penalized GLM, and Survival Regression (AFT).

Note on quantile_summary: Quantile regression has no analytic standard errors, so the std_error, statistic, and p_value columns are returned as NaN. The coefficient estimates themselves are still valid.

Note on ridge_summary (lambda_ > 0): std_error is the ridge sandwich standard error (sigma^2 * A @ X'X @ A', matching R), but statistic/p_value are NaN — a classical t-test on shrunken/biased coefficients is not statistically valid (anofox-regression 0.5.14 #37). lambda_ = 0 delegates fully to OLS inference (statistic/p_value populated). See Ridge for the class-level equivalent.

Note on negative_binomial_summary's estimate_dispersion: scales std_error by the Pearson chi2/df dispersion estimate (R summary.glm semantics); default False keeps dispersion fixed at 1.0. See NegativeBinomial.

Note on rls_summary's initial_p_diagonal: sets the initial covariance prior P0 = initial_p_diagonal * I; default 1e6 is identical to omitting it. See RLS.

alias_tolerance (0.8.0, ols_summary/wls_summary): R lm's configurable rank-deficiency tolerance, default 1e-7. A later column that is a linear combination of the intercept and earlier kept columns within this tolerance is aliased (NaN estimate/ std_error/statistic/p_value for that term). See Linear Models and Rank-deficient designs.

GLM intercept inference since 0.8.0 (anofox-regression 0.5.20 #66): every GLM *_summary (logistic_summary, poisson_summary, negative_binomial_summary, tweedie_summary, probit_summary, cloglog_summary) now reports the intercept row's std_error/statistic/p_value (previously NaN). tweedie_summary additionally reports t-based statistics/p-values (t on the residual df, as R's summary.glm) for every row, where they previously could be NaN. The Gamma PyModel's std_errors/p_values getters gained the same t-based values (no gamma_summary expression exists yet).

Returns: See Summary Output

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
# Get coefficient table per group
df.group_by("group").agg(
    ps.ols_summary("y", "x1", "x2").alias("coef")
).explode("coef").unnest("coef")

Output: | group | term | estimate | std_error | statistic | p_value | |-------|------|----------|-----------|-----------|---------| | A | intercept | 1.234 | 0.123 | 10.03 | 0.000 | | A | x1 | 0.567 | 0.045 | 12.60 | 0.000 | | A | x2 | -0.234 | 0.067 | -3.49 | 0.001 |

docs.title: Prediction Functions
docs.text: Return per-row predictions with optional confidence/prediction intervals.

docs.title: Signature
docs.text:
ps.ols_predict(
    y: Union[pl.Expr, str],
    *x: Union[pl.Expr, str],
    add_intercept: bool = True,
    interval: str | None = None,  # None, "confidence", "prediction"
    level: float = 0.95,
    null_policy: str = "drop",    # "drop", "drop_y_zero_x"
    alias_tolerance: float = 1e-7,
) -> pl.Expr

ols_predict/wls_predict also accept alias_tolerance (default 1e-7) — same rank-deficiency tolerance as ols/wls (see the note above); a column aliased at fit time contributes NaN to the prediction wherever that column is involved.

docs.title: Available Functions
docs.text:
All models have prediction functions: - ols_predict, ridge_predict, elastic_net_predict - wls_predict, rls_predict, bls_predict, nnls_predict - logistic_predict, poisson_predict, negative_binomial_predict - tweedie_predict, probit_predict, cloglog_predict - alm_predict - quantile_predict, isotonic_predict, lm_dynamic_predict - penalized_glm_predict (predict_type="response" or "link") - aft_predict_quantile, aft_predict_median, aft_predict_survival, aft_predict_cdf

Formula variants also available: ps.ols_formula_predict(formula, ...), etc.

penalized_glm_predict/aft_predict_* have no analytic intervals — lower/upper are always NaN; neither FittedPenalizedGlm nor FittedAft has an interval-prediction method upstream. See Penalized GLM and Survival Regression (AFT) for the full parameter lists (predict_type/null_policy for the former; p/t/null_policy for the latter's four variants).

Models without analytic intervals. The following predictors return lower / upper as NaN — point predictions only:

Function Why no intervals quantile_predict Quantile regression intervals require bootstrap (not yet wired through). isotonic_predict Step-function fit with no parametric uncertainty estimate. lm_dynamic_predict Predictions use time-averaged coefficients from the dynamic model. penalized_glm_predict FittedPenalizedGlm has no interval-prediction method upstream. aft_predict_quantile/_median/_survival/_cdf FittedAft has no interval-prediction method upstream.

ridge_predict's intervals use the sandwich variance factor (anofox-regression 0.5.14 #37): interval="confidence"/"prediction" widths are computed from the ridge sandwich covariance (A @ X'X @ A'), which is narrower than the pre-0.8.0 interval width for lambda_ > 0.

negative_binomial_predict/negative_binomial_summary accept estimate_dispersion (default False) — see the Summary Functions note above. Note: negative_binomial_predict itself has no theta kwarg (theta is always estimated for prediction).

rls_predict/rls_summary accept initial_p_diagonal (default 1e6) — see the Summary Functions note above.

# Quantile regression predictions
df.with_columns(
    ps.quantile_predict("y", "x1", "x2", tau=0.5).over("group").alias("p")
).unnest("p")

# Isotonic step-function predictions (single feature)
df.with_columns(
    ps.isotonic_predict("y", "x").alias("p")
).unnest("p")

# Dynamic linear model predictions
df.with_columns(
    ps.lm_dynamic_predict("y", "x1", "x2").over("group").alias("p")
).unnest("p")

Returns: See Prediction Output

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Description interval None (point only), "confidence" (mean interval), "prediction" (individual interval) level Confidence level (default 0.95 for 95% intervals) null_policy How to handle missing values: "drop" or "drop_y_zero_x"

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
# Per-group predictions with 95% prediction intervals
df.with_columns(
    ps.ols_predict("y", "x1", "x2", interval="prediction", level=0.95)
        .over("group").alias("pred")
).unnest("pred")

Output: | group | y | x1 | x2 | prediction | lower | upper | |-------|---|----|----|------------|-------|-------| | A | 5.2 | 1.0 | 2.0 | 5.15 | 3.21 | 7.09 | | A | 3.8 | 0.5 | 1.5 | 3.92 | 1.98 | 5.86 |

docs.title: Interval Types
docs.text:
Type Description Use Case None Point prediction only Fast prediction "confidence" Interval for mean response Uncertainty about regression line "prediction" Interval for individual observation Forecasting new observations

Note: Prediction intervals are always wider than confidence intervals because they account for both uncertainty in the regression line and individual observation variance.

docs.title: Survival Regression (AFT)
docs.text:
Accelerated failure time (AFT) survival regression with right censoring, for any of the Weibull, log-normal, log-logistic or exponential error distributions. Validated against R survival::survreg on the anofox-regression 0.5.22 R reference fixture (all four distributions).

Works with group_by and .over().

docs.title: Model
docs.text: AFT models log T = x'beta + sigma * W for a fixed error distribution W — the same parametrisation R's survival::survreg uses. An observation contributes its density when the event was observed and its survival probability when the row is still censored.

docs.title: Distributions
docs.text:
distribution Aliases Scale (sigma) "weibull" — Estimated "lognormal" "log_normal", "log-normal" Estimated "loglogistic" "log_logistic", "log-logistic" Estimated "exponential" "exp" Fixed at 1.0 (not estimated)

An unknown distribution raises ValueError when the expression is built — before .collect().

docs.title: Event Coding
docs.text:
event is the right-censoring indicator, positionally after time:

  • True/1 — an observed event.
  • False/0 — a right-censored observation.
  • Accepts a Boolean column directly, or a numeric column containing only 0/1. Any other value — including R's 1/2 coding — fails the whole fit rather than being silently misread.

time must be strictly positive; a non-positive or non-finite time fails the whole fit (returned as all-NaN). A null time or a null event drops that row from the fit. Rows with a null/non-finite value in any feature are also dropped before fitting.

docs.title: aft
docs.text:
ps.aft(
    time: Union[pl.Expr, str],
    event: Union[pl.Expr, str],
    *x: Union[pl.Expr, str],
    distribution: Literal["weibull", "exponential", "lognormal", "loglogistic"] = "weibull",
    priors: Sequence[None | str | tuple | dict] | None = None,
    add_intercept: bool = True,
    max_iter: int = 100,
    tol: float = 1e-9,
) -> pl.Expr
Parameter Description time Event or censoring time; must be strictly positive event Right-censoring indicator; see Event Coding distribution Error distribution for T; see Distributions priors Per-coefficient priors, positionally aligned with x. Same format as penalized_glm's priors add_intercept Whether to include an intercept term max_iter Maximum Newton iterations tol Convergence tolerance on the log-likelihood

Returns: Struct — see AFT Output for the full 12-field schema (intercept, coefficients, scale, log_likelihood, null_log_likelihood, aic, bic, iterations, converged, n_observations, n_events, n_censored).

import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import polars_statistics as ps

np.random.seed(1)
n = 80
x1 = np.random.normal(0, 1, n)
x2 = np.random.normal(0, 1, n)
scale = 0.7
eta = 1.0 + 0.5 * x1 - 0.3 * x2
log_t = eta + scale * np.random.gumbel(size=n)  # extreme-value errors -> Weibull AFT
time = np.exp(log_t)
censor_time = np.random.exponential(scale=np.median(time) * 1.5, size=n)
observed_time = np.minimum(time, censor_time)
event = (time <= censor_time).astype(float)

df = pl.DataFrame(
    {"group": ["A"] * n, "time": observed_time, "event": event, "x1": x1, "x2": x2}
)

result = df.group_by("group").agg(
    ps.aft("time", "event", "x1", "x2", distribution="weibull").alias("model")
)
print(result)

docs.title: aft_summary
docs.text:
ps.aft_summary(
    time: Union[pl.Expr, str],
    event: Union[pl.Expr, str],
    *x: Union[pl.Expr, str],
    distribution: Literal["weibull", "exponential", "lognormal", "loglogistic"] = "weibull",
    priors: Sequence[None | str | tuple | dict] | None = None,
    vcov_type: Literal["laplace", "sandwich", "naive"] = "laplace",
    conf_level: float = 0.95,
    add_intercept: bool = True,
    max_iter: int = 100,
    tol: float = 1e-9,
) -> pl.Expr

Rows are intercept (when add_intercept=True), x1..xp, then log_scale (omitted for distribution="exponential", whose scale is fixed at 1 and not estimated).

Returns: List[Struct] with columns term, estimate, std_error, statistic, p_value, ci_lower, ci_upper — the shared 7-field tidy summary schema, also used by penalized_glm_summary. The intercept row is read directly from upstream's AftInference intercept fields, never recomputed locally; the log_scale row's statistic/p_value/CI are computed from upstream's log_scale_std_error using the identical Wald formula (z = estimate / std_error, p = 2 * (1 - Phi(|z|))). See Inference Summary Output.

import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import polars_statistics as ps

np.random.seed(1)
n = 80
x1 = np.random.normal(0, 1, n)
x2 = np.random.normal(0, 1, n)
scale = 0.7
eta = 1.0 + 0.5 * x1 - 0.3 * x2
log_t = eta + scale * np.random.gumbel(size=n)
time = np.exp(log_t)
censor_time = np.random.exponential(scale=np.median(time) * 1.5, size=n)
observed_time = np.minimum(time, censor_time)
event = (time <= censor_time).astype(float)

df = pl.DataFrame({"time": observed_time, "event": event, "x1": x1, "x2": x2})

result = df.select(
    ps.aft_summary("time", "event", "x1", "x2", distribution="weibull").alias("s")
).explode("s").unnest("s")
print(result)

docs.title: aft_predict_quantile
docs.text:
ps.aft_predict_quantile(
    time: Union[pl.Expr, str],
    event: Union[pl.Expr, str],
    *x: Union[pl.Expr, str],
    p: float = 0.5,
    distribution: Literal["weibull", "exponential", "lognormal", "loglogistic"] = "weibull",
    priors: Sequence[None | str | tuple | dict] | None = None,
    add_intercept: bool = True,
    max_iter: int = 100,
    tol: float = 1e-9,
    null_policy: Literal["drop", "drop_y_zero_x"] = "drop",
    name: str | None = None,
) -> pl.Expr

Predicted p-quantile of the survival time. Refits per group/.over() partition with the same options used for aft, then predicts on every row.

null_policy="drop" (default) gives a NaN prediction for a row with a null/non-finite time, event, or feature. null_policy="drop_y_zero_x" excludes a null-time/event row from the fit but still predicts it (unlike penalized_glm_predict's offset, event is fit-only data — not required predict input, since the four predict expressions only read x).

Returns: Struct with {name}_prediction/{name}_lower/{name}_upper (default name="aft_predict_quantile"). lower/upper are always NaN — the upstream engine has no interval-prediction method.

import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import polars_statistics as ps

np.random.seed(1)
n = 80
x1 = np.random.normal(0, 1, n)
x2 = np.random.normal(0, 1, n)
scale = 0.7
eta = 1.0 + 0.5 * x1 - 0.3 * x2
log_t = eta + scale * np.random.gumbel(size=n)
time = np.exp(log_t)
censor_time = np.random.exponential(scale=np.median(time) * 1.5, size=n)
observed_time = np.minimum(time, censor_time)
event = (time <= censor_time).astype(float)

df = pl.DataFrame({"group": ["A"] * n, "time": observed_time, "event": event, "x1": x1, "x2": x2})

result = df.with_columns(
    ps.aft_predict_quantile("time", "event", "x1", "x2", p=0.9, distribution="weibull")
        .over("group").alias("pred")
).unnest("pred")
print(result.head(3))

import polars as pl
import polars_statistics as ps

    ps.aft_formula_predict_survival(

    ).alias("pred")
).unnest("pred")

docs.text: Coefficients/scale (1e-6), log-likelihoods (1e-7), and intercept/coefficient/log(scale) standard errors (1e-5) are validated against R's survival::survreg on the anofox-regression 0.5.22 R reference fixture, across all four distributions (Weibull, log-normal, log-logistic, exponential).
